clips.text: This is not a channel about art. This is not about architecture. And this is not about culture as entertainment. This is about what all of this actually means. Because culture is never only culture. It is a signal of capital, of status, of power, the spaces you enter, the objects you see, the events you attend, the institutions you trust. None of it is random. It is structured, encoded, and understood by those who know how to read it. Code decodes the signals of capital, culture, and power. This is code.

clips.text: He didn't design buildings. He designed whether the city could stand. In 1975, New York City was close to collapse. Not visually, structurally. It was running out of money. Unable to finance itself. Unable to function. Felix Rohaten was not an architect. He was an investment banker. But what he built was closer to architecture than finance. He helped create the Municipal Assistance Corporation. A structure. It could issue bonds, restructure debt, control flows of capital, money became framework, debt became material. The city was no longer governed only by policy. It was stabilized by design. Budgets were no longer political statements. They were engineered constraints. This is the architecture. A system where capital defines what can continue to exist. Rohaton didn't fund the city. He restructured its possibility. This is the code. Power is not always visible in form. Sometimes it exists in the conditions that allow form to remain, not architecture, but structural.

clips.text: This is not a story about a lawyer. It's a story about how conflict becomes method. Roy Cohn entered American public life early. In 1953 and 1954, he served as chief counsel to Senator Joseph McCarthy's investigations. That period matters. Not because it explains everything, but because it reveals a method, pressure, exposure, counter-attack. Years later, Here in New York, the same logic appears in a different system, not in Washington, in real estate, in media, in public dispute. By the 1970s, Donald Trump was moving within a world where Roy Cohn had already learned how systems respond under pressure. Cohn's principle was direct, never apologize, never concede the frame. If attacked, attack harder. The objective was not always to win. It was to redefine the conditions under which the conflict is understood. This is where the structure becomes visible. Legal conflict stops being only legal. It becomes narrative. It becomes positioning. It becomes presence. What moved forward was not advice. It was a transferable structure. Pressure instead of retreat. Visibility instead of resolution. Counterattack instead of explanation. and what moves forward is rarely visible at the moment it happens. A conversation, a method, a way of responding. At the time it appears small, almost procedural, years later it begins to appear elsewhere, in different contexts, at different scales, not as memory as pattern. That is why this matters, not because one individual defined it, but because methods like this outlive the people who carry them, and once absorbed, they stop looking personal. They start looking structural, not a defense, not an accusation, a pattern that continues to reorganize outcomes.

clips.text: This is not advertising. This is how behavior gets engineered. His name was Edward Bernays, the nephew of Sigmund Freud. He didn't sell products. He rewired what people believed they wanted. In the early 20th century, markets had a problem. Production was growing faster than demand. People didn't need more things. So the question changed. Not how to sell, but how to make people want. In 1929, women smoking in public was still taboo. Bernays reframed it. He staged a public event in New York. Young women walking and smoking during the Easter parade. He called cigarettes torches of freedom. The product didn't change. The meaning did. Smoking became a symbol of independence. Sales followed. Bacon was not a standard breakfast. Bernays changed that. He consulted a physician then sent letters to over 5,000 doctors. The question was framed carefully. Is a heavier breakfast healthier than a light one? The majority agreed. That consensus was published. Bacon and eggs became not a preference, a recommendation. Women were starting to abandon hair nets. Demand dropped. Bernays reframed the issue as hygiene. Hair restraint was presented as a matter of cleanliness, not style. Industries aligned behind the message. Hairnets returned, not as fashion, but as necessity. Shared drinking cups were common. Bernays made them unacceptable. Public messaging emphasized contamination. Germs became visible, conceptually. Disposable cups became not convenience, but safety. A new habit was installed. Soap is a commodity, hard to differentiate. Bernays turned it into activity. He organized children's competitions, sculptures made from soap. The product entered the home not as hygiene only, but as play. Usage increased, not through persuasion, through integration into behavior. For United Fruit Company, Bernay shaped perception of entire country. He framed Guatemala as politically unstable and threatening. Media narratives followed. Public opinion shifted. Policy followed. This was no longer consumption. This was environment control. Across all cases, the mechanism repeats. Not product, but association. Not need, but meaning. Not choice, but context. Bernays called it, engineering of consent. Not forcing behavior. Structuring the conditions under which behavior feels natural. This is the code. People don't adopt products. They adopt the stories attached to them.

clips.text: LACMA just opened. But this is not an opening. It's a shift. When a museum stops being a museum, on April 19, 2026, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art opened the David Geffen Galleries, a project nearly a decade in the making, approximately $724 million, designed by Peter Zumthor, partly funded by a $150 million contribution from David Geffen. But the numbers are not the point. Architecture as a statement. It refuses the familiar logic of the museum. museum. No clear chronology. No geographic divisions. No schools. No periods. Instead, a single continuous space of approximately 110,000 square feet, elevated above ground, crossing Wilshire Boulevard. Not rooms. A flow. This is not architecture of storage. It is architecture of curating perception. To build it, the museum removed what existed before. The Echmanston Building, 1965. The Hammer of institutional structure replaced by a different logic. Which raises a quiet question. Did the museum expand? Or did it reduce itself? Because the display space did not increase proportionally, and much of the collection remains unseen. The response has been divided. For some, this is a necessary break. A move beyond Eurocentric narratives. A museum of the 21st century. For others, it is a loss of context. A dissolution of structure. A building that speaks louder than the works it holds. But the deeper shift is internal. Traditionally, a museum did three things. It preserved, it classified, it explained, now it mixes, it compares, it places side by side, and that changes everything. Because when chronology disappears, when geography dissolves, when the canon is no longer explicit, order does not disappear, it becomes invisible, and still determines what you see, which is where the museum becomes something else. Not a repository, not an educational platform, but a system of attention distribution. And this is not an isolated case. Museums are beginning to compete with media, to work with attention rather than objects, to construct narratives rather than histories. This is not about art. It is about the architecture of perception. Insiders note something else. The entire building operates as a single span elevated structure with no internal columns in the main gallery, which means every placement is a decision, not a constraint. Climate control is uniform across the floor, allowing works from different periods and materials to be placed in proximity that would traditionally be separated. And the circulation path is intentionally non-linear. There is no prescribed beginning, no official end. Which removes sequence, but not influence. And that brings us back to the shift. The question used to be, what does the museum show? Now, it is something else. How does it make you see it?

clips.text: This is not a debate about AI. It is a shift in who controls cultural reality, January 27, 2026. The British Museum publishes AI-generated images on its official channels. Days later, it deletes them after backlash. Not because they were unrealistic, because they were too acceptable. Archaeologists and researchers warned this is not just visual experimentation, It risks replacing human interpretation with synthetic approximation, and once institutions normalize that, they redefine authority itself, but the market had already moved. February 20th to March 5th, 2025, Christie's runs its first AI-only auction. Augmented intelligence. More than 30 lots. Artists. Refik Anadol. Holly Herndon. Matt Dryhurst. Claire Silver. Estimated over $600,000. Before the sale even opened, over 3,500 artists signed an open letter demanding cancellation. The claim, AI models were trained on copyrighted works without consent, not innovation, extraction. Christie's response was precise. These are established artists using AI as a tool. The sale goes ahead. said. Final result, $728.784. Top lot, Refic Anadol's Machine Hallucinations, ISS Dreams, A sold for $270.00, $200. And something else happened, 37% of bidders were completely new to Christie's. Nearly half were millennials and Gen Z. The market did not reject AI, it expanded through it. Meanwhile another part of the system reacted differently. Finally, January 22, 2026, San Diego Comic Con officially bans AI-generated art from its art show. Not a debate. A rule. At the same time in Denmark, robot artist Aida presents Spacepod, a conceptual architecture for extraterrestrial habitats. A machine not just generating images but proposing environments. So this is not one story, it is three systems colliding. marketing, the market accepts, institutions hesitate, gatekeepers restrict, and underneath all of it, one question becomes unavoidable. If art can be generated, curated, and distributed without human authorship, who exactly is shaping what we see, and more importantly, will we even notice when that answer changes?

clips.text: Amalakobuwafo is not just a painter. He is a test case. Born in 1984 in Acra, trained in Vienna, he developed a distinctive technique, painting portraits with his fingers. By the late 2010s, the work was already recognizable, but recognition is not the same as acceleration. That came later. In 2019, at Art Basel Miami Beach, Gallery Marianne Ibrahim presented his solo booth. At the same time, the Rubel Museum not only acquired his work but made him artist-in-residence and the city of Miami Beach acquired a painting through its legacy purchase program which meant that even before the auction surge the artist received what the market values most highly not just demand but the combination of fair momentum institutional validation and a collector signal then the timeline compressed February 2020 the lemon bathing suit sells for $881.500 almost immediately the narrative changes, not just a promising painter, a market event. By 2021-2022, the signals intensify. December 2021, Christie's Hong Kong hands up sells for approximately 3.42 million. March 2022, Christie's London yellow blanket reaches 1.24 million against an estimate of $400,000 to $600,000. Other results followed. Purple on red at Phillips $750,000 lighter at $325,000 dollars against a $40,000 to $60,000 estimate. At this point, the question becomes difficult to avoid what exactly was being priced, the painting or the convergence around it, because Boafo sits at a precise intersection, a highly recognizable visual language, a renewed market interest in figuration, institutional attention to black portraiture, and rapid gallery amplification. The market did not discover him slowly. It received a fully assembled signal, fare, museum, collector, auction, media, and then it moved, which is why some critics describe such trajectories as speculative, not because the work lacks substance, but because price acceleration begins to outpace the time required for institutional and critical consolidation. There is context for that. Auction sales of artists born in Africa peaked at $197 million in 2022, then declined to $113.4 million in 2023 and $77.2 million in 2024, not collapse, but deceleration. And yet, the story does not end there, because outside the market, Boafo is building something else. In Accra, he develops a residency and cultural infrastructure project, which introduces another question. Can a market-driven rise still produce a long-term institutional base? Or are these two timelines fundamentally different? Today, his auction prices have cooled from their peak. The works still sell, the exhibitions continue, the visibility remains, but at a different altitude. Which leads to a final question. Where exactly is the line between recognition and construction? Who draws it?

clips.text: Before we call it speculation, it's worth remembering. Art was never outside the market. What we now describe as volatility once operated as proto-market structures. What we call branding was already early reputation engineering. And what looks like patronage functioned as capital deployment. Take Florence, early 1500s. When the Medici Commission work, they weren't buying images. They were structuring visibility. contract specified everything, scale, subject, delivery timelines, even pigment. Ultramarine, ground from Lapis Lazuli imported from Afghanistan, was often more expensive than gold. In several renaissance contracts its use was explicitly negotiated, not for aesthetics, but as a marker of the patron's financial reach. Domenico Girlandaio's commissions, for example, included clauses on material hierarchy. And in 1508, Michelangelo's Sistine Chapel Agreement with Pope Julius II defined not just the theme, but the scope, sequence, and payment structure tied to completion. Leonardo da Vinci's Virgin of the Rocks became the subject of a legal dispute over delivery, pricing, and contractual expectations. This wasn't freedom. It was a commission-based signaling system, where artists executed and patrons encoded power through images. The Medici didn't just support art, they engineered perception. They understood that images circulate reputation faster than capital alone. So when we say that art has become financial, we're not describing a rupture, we're describing continuity. Only the language changed, the system didn't arrive, it refined itself.
